packs.title: Circles, Fragments and Open Space
packs.promise: Find another Vienna through garden structures, tree-lined space and uneven facades.

q.s: Collect a palette from a broad facade.
st: Find three colour ingredients from one stopped view: the ochre-yellow wall, pale trim and a dark window.
Give each colour a name of your own and arrange the three names from lightest to darkest. A rough drawing works too.
Save your palette and one repeated shape you would pair with it. Leave signs, tickets and other visitors out of any optional photo.

q.s: Collect a whole shape and two interruptions.
st: Find a rounded arch, a broken upper edge and a rectangular pool edge from one comfortable view. Leave all stonework untouched.
Give the arch one word suggesting continuity and each interrupted edge one word suggesting a break.
Save the three words together and note which interruption is easiest to notice. Do not climb, step over a barrier or approach the pool for a closer view.

q.s: Collect three edges around a street corner.
st: Find three shapes around the square from one stopped view: a rounded building corner, a straight window edge and a branching tree outline.
Give each shape one short description and arrange the three descriptions from the most regular to the least regular.
Save the sequence and one reason for your order. Leave passing people and café customers out of any optional photo.

packs.title: Between Ornament and Pause
packs.promise: Find Vienna in a flourish, a contrast, and a pause of your own.

q.s: Turn a tiled pattern into a tiny visual rhythm.
st: Stop in a roomy place on Stephansplatz where part of the cathedral’s patterned tiled roof is visible. Keep the cathedral entrances clear.
Find a short sequence that repeats: a change of colour, a zigzag, or the edge between two bands. Follow only a small patch rather than trying to read the whole roof.
Give the sequence three or four silent beats using simple words such as light, dark, light, turn. Change your words until they match the pattern you see.
Save your roof rhythm with one sentence about the detail that made you look twice.

q.s: Let a quiet facade answer a more elaborate neighbour.
st: Choose a public stopping place on Michaelerplatz where you can compare the Looshaus with part of the Hofburg facade. Stay out of carriage and vehicle routes.
Find one deliberate contrast: plain upper windows against ornament, a flat plane against a curve, or a restrained surface against a dramatic entrance.
Write a two-line conversation. Let one building make a claim about the detail you chose, and let the other answer in its own imagined voice.
Add a final word explaining which side you would join today. Your buildings can disagree gently; no architectural expertise is needed.

q.s: Give glass and greenery a line each.
st: During the garden’s posted opening hours, choose a comfortable public path or bench with a view of the Palmenhaus and nearby planting.

Notice one quality of the glass-and-metal building and one contrasting quality of a tree, leaf or patch of planting. Keep the comparison specific: straight and branching, reflective and matte, repeated and irregular.
Write a postcard in two short lines. Give the built material the first line and the living material the second; use your own words instead of describing all of Vienna.
Finish with a small title that joins your two details. Keep the postcard as your memory of this garden edge.
